# Data & code sharing {#data-sharing}

TADA is about your code. This chapter covers everything sitting around it: what
data to share, in what format, with what metadata, under what licence, and what
a journal will check.

::: {.tada-note}
**On this page:** [what archiving is for](#sharing-goals) · [vocabulary](#sharing-glossary) · [what data to share](#sharing-what) · [file formats](#sharing-formats) · [metadata](#sharing-metadata) · [licences](#sharing-licences) · [the SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) · [advice for authors](#sharing-authors) · [checklist](#sharing-checklist)
:::

## What archiving is for {#sharing-goals}

This is worth stating explicitly, because the three goals pull in slightly
different directions and different practices serve each one. The SORTEE
guidelines set out three:

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[1]{.tada-letter} [Data reuse]{.tada-word}
[Prevents data loss; enables research synthesis and meta-analysis; allows
re-analysis as methods improve; and allows new questions to be asked of existing
data, which in turn **reduces the number of animals used in
experiments**.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[2]{.tada-letter} [Transparency]{.tada-word}
[Readers can see what was actually done to obtain the reported results. Open
data will not stop fabrication, but it makes fabrication far easier to
detect.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[3]{.tada-letter} [Computational reproducibility]{.tada-word}
[Someone else can reproduce the published results from the archived data and
code.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

Two further points from the guidelines are easy to miss:

- **Data are typically collected with public money**, and so can be seen as a
  public good that should not be lost when a researcher changes job or a
  computer breaks. Lost data and code represent a substantial source of research
  waste.
- Published results are often **not described in enough detail to be included in
  a meta-analysis**. Archiving the data lets a synthesist re-analyse them to get
  what they need, and substantially increases the evidence available for
  synthesis.

## Vocabulary {#sharing-glossary}

Key terms from the SORTEE glossary (Table 1), because these terms are used
loosely and the distinctions matter when someone asks you for "the raw data".

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Metadata** | A description of, and information about, the data and code. Typically a text file called a README; variants include a codebook or a data dictionary. |
| **Raw data** | Unprocessed and unfiltered data, including any raw files such as photos, audio recordings, videos and data sheets. |
| **Data filtering** | Removing some data to create the dataset used in the analysis, for example removing individuals with a certain characteristic. The result is **filtered data**. |
| **Data processing** | Transforming data from one form to another: extraction from images or video, summarising, transforming, calculating. The result is **processed data**. |
| **Repository** | A framework providing long-term storage for many projects, such as Zenodo, Dryad or Figshare. |
| **Project** | A collection of files archived for a specific manuscript. This is similar to what GitHub calls a *repository*, which is the source of some confusion. |
| **Data editor** | An editorial position at a journal, responsible for screening and quality-controlling the data and code archived alongside manuscripts under review. |
| **Data and code quality control** | Checking the suitability of data and code for public archiving. |

::: {.tada-note}
Transcribing data from a written to a digital format, and the error-checking
that follows, does **not** count as processing. A typed-up field sheet is still
raw data.
:::

## What data to share {#sharing-what}

Ideally, **both raw and processed data**. The SORTEE guidelines state that
ideally both raw and processed data are provided, and allow three acceptable
forms, with (b) and (c) as fallbacks where a full raw upload is not possible:

**a)** Raw data, along with the processed data and/or the code to prepare the
data for analysis.

**b)** A **sample** of raw data alongside the processed and filtered data, when
a full raw data upload is not possible.

**c)** Processed and filtered data with a **detailed description of how to both
obtain and process or filter the raw data**.

Raw data matter because without them nobody can check the filtering and
processing steps, which is where undetected errors most often originate. Option
(c) is acceptable, but it places the whole burden on your written description
being complete.

## File formats {#sharing-formats}

The rule is the same for data as for code: **universally interoperable**,
meaning the file can be exchanged and used across different software and
operating systems.

::: {.tabset}

### Data formats {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**Prefer simple text-based formats.** `.csv`, `.tsv` and `.txt` can be used by
more software, across more systems, than anything else.

| Format | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` | **Preferred.** Maximally interoperable. |
| `.parquet` | Interoperable, highly compressed, efficiently read, and highly accurate for large datasets. |
| `.xlsx` | Not proprietary, so interoperable, but can carry information such as formatting that is **lost on import** into statistical software. |
| `.xls` | Proprietary format. Avoid. |
| `.RData`, `.rds` | Usable with open-source software, but requires knowledge of R to extract, and may depend on the R version used to save it. Restricts reuse. |
| `.sps` and other proprietary formats | Not interoperable; do not facilitate reuse. |
| `.pdf`, `.docx` | **Never.** Prone to error when copy-pasted, and cannot be readily imported into statistical programs. |

::: {.tada-note}
SPSS `.sps` files appear here as unsuitable, yet [Transferable](#tada-languages)
gives them as an example of a file type that passes. Both are correct, because
they are judging different things: this table concerns **data** files, where
`.sps` is a proprietary format, whereas the Transferable test concerns **code**
files, where an `.sps` syntax file can at least be opened in a text editor.
:::

Where there is genuinely no alternative, as with data collected by proprietary
software, provide the non-interoperable file **alongside interoperable extracted
data**, with a clear description of the conversion process in the metadata,
**including the software version used**.

### Code formats {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code must be in a format that can be readily opened by text editors and IDEs
such as VS Code: `.R`, `.py`, `.cpp`, and so on. See
[Transferable](#transferable-filetype).

**Code must not be provided as a `.pdf` or pasted into a Word document.** Even
where the script can be copied and pasted out, these programs often insert
additional characters or spacing that the analysis software misinterprets. The
canonical example is Python code that fails to run because the indentation was
mangled.

:::

## Metadata: what a README must contain {#sharing-metadata}

The [Documented](#documented-readme) chapter covers the code README in detail.
The SORTEE guidelines set out what is needed on the **data** side, and the two
overlap heavily.

**General information**

- Manuscript title and abstract
- Authors and relevant contact information
- Date and location of data collection
- A list of all relevant funders
- Licence information, for example CC-BY
- Information about data derived from other sources, such as other articles or
  online data

**Detailed file descriptions**

- What each data file contains and how it is structured
- What variables it contains
- **What units of measurement they are in**
- How they link to the data described in the manuscript, so that every column in
  a `.csv` is explained and described

Deliver this as part of the main README, as separate README files describing the
data and code, or as a **data dictionary** per data file, for example a `.csv`
with one column for variable names and another for their descriptions.

::: {.tada-key}
The bar the guidelines set for both data and code metadata is the word
**"adequate"**: metadata detailed enough that **anyone can understand the data,
or the analysis code, without needing to read the manuscript**. A README that
only makes sense alongside your methods section does not meet that bar.
:::

::: {.tada-note}
Under double-blind review, some sections can be **left blank until acceptance**
and filled in then.
:::

**On LLMs.** The SORTEE guidelines add that the README should state **whether
and how the authors have used large language models in code generation**
([Resnik & Hosseini 2025]{.tada-cite key="resnik-2025"}), while
noting that a data editor is unlikely to be able to verify this.

## Licences {#sharing-licences}

Without a licence, data and code **cannot be legally reused** in many
circumstances, depending on jurisdiction. Most researchers have little knowledge
of licences, so this is a common and consequential gap.

::: {.tabset}

### For data {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Typically **Creative Commons** licences. Chooser:
<https://creativecommons.org/chooser/>

| Licence | What it means | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **CC0** | Public domain; no attribution required | The most permissive. Default at Figshare; **mandated by Dryad**. |
| **CC BY 4.0** | Reusers must credit the original author, but may distribute, remix, adapt and build upon the material, including commercially | Default at Zenodo. |
| **CC BY-NC 4.0** | As CC BY, but prohibits commercial use | More restrictive. |

### For code {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Software licences rather than Creative Commons. Chooser:
<https://choosealicense.com/>

| Licence | What it means |
|---|---|
| **MIT** | Very permissive: copy, modify, merge, publish and share, with the licence notice retained |
| **BSD 2-Clause / 3-Clause** | Permissive, similar in spirit to MIT |
| **Apache 2.0** | Permissive, with an explicit patent grant |
| **GPL v3.0** | Copyleft: derivatives must carry the same licence, and changes from the source must be listed |

The SORTEE guidelines suggest permissive code licences wherever possible,
naming MIT, BSD 2-Clause, GNU and Apache (Stage 3.2).

CC0 is **not well suited to code**, which is why Dryad, being CC0-only, points
code deposits at Zenodo.

### Choosing {.unlisted .unnumbered}

The SORTEE guidelines treat data and code differently. For **data** they
**do not recommend or enforce any specific type of licence**, so the requirement
is simply that you choose one and state it. For **code** they suggest
**permissive licences wherever possible**, naming MIT, BSD 2-Clause, GNU and
Apache (Stage 3.2).

Four further things should influence the choice:

- Who the audience is, and whether commercial application is expected
- Whether you want others to be able to modify or extend the work
- What your **journal, institution and funder** require, since some journals
  mandate a licence on archiving; the *Journal of Statistical Software* requires
  a GPL
- Whether your **repository** already applies one by default, or mandates one

In practice: pick a licence at <https://choosealicense.com/>, copy the licence
text into a `LICENSE` file in the project, and name it in the README. Or select
it in the repository's deposit form, as Zenodo allows.

:::

## The SORTEE guidelines {#sortee}

The **SORTEE guidelines for data and code quality control** ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite key="pick-2026"},
*Peer Community Journal* 6: e20) are written for **data editors**, the editorial
role responsible for screening and quality-controlling data and code at a
journal. They are worth reading as an author precisely because they tell you
what will be checked.

::: {.tada-note}
**The limits of quality control.** It is about ensuring archived data and code
meet minimum standards: complete, usable, documented and runnable. It is
explicitly **not** a code review. A data editor does not critique your
analytical techniques, and it is not their role to review, interpret or correct
your code, nor to check its reliability
([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite key="ivimey-cook-2023"}; [Hillemann et al. 2025]{.tada-cite key="hillemann-2025"}). That is what
[code review](#code-review) is for.
:::

### The six stages {#sortee-stages}

Table 2 of the paper is reproduced in full below.

| Stage | Guideline |
|---|---|
| **1. Data must be archived and adhere to FAIR guiding principles** | |
| 1.1 Data files are accessible and in an open repository | Data are open and freely available and are located in a permanent public repository with an associated globally unique persistent identifier, that is cited in the text and reference list of the manuscript. |
| 1.2 Data are associated with a license | Data must be associated with a license. |
| 1.3 Data files are present and complete | Authors must either provide: a) raw data, along with the processed data and/or code to prepare the data for analysis, or b) a sample of raw data alongside processed/filtered data when full raw data upload is not possible, or c) processed/filtered data with a detailed description of how to both obtain and process/filter the raw data. |
| 1.4 Data files are in an interoperable format | Data files must be provided in an interoperable format. |
| 1.5 Data metadata is present and adequate | Detailed metadata, including (but not limited to) a README file, must accompany the data. |
| **2. Archived data corresponds with the data reported in the manuscript** | The structure and contents of the archived data files must match the description in the manuscript. |
| **3. Code must be archived and adhere to FAIR guiding principles** | |
| 3.1 Code files are accessible and in an open repository | Code files are open and freely available and are located in a permanent public repository with an associated globally unique persistent identifier, preferably in the same archived project as the data files, and are cited in the text and the reference list of the manuscript. |
| 3.2 Code is associated with a license | The code must be associated with a license. |
| 3.3 Code files are present and complete | All code used for generating the results of the manuscript (including filtering, processing, graphing, and analysis) must be present either in one or more code files. |
| 3.4 Code is in an interoperable format | Code files must be provided in an interoperable format. |
| 3.5 Code metadata is present and adequate | A sufficiently detailed README must accompany the code. Code must also be broken into sections with clear annotation stating the purpose of the code with clear links to the relevant sections, figures, and tables in the manuscript. |
| **4. Archived code corresponds with the workflow reported in the manuscript** | The structure and content of the archived code must match the description of data filtering, processing, and analysis, and the presentation of results in the manuscript. |
| **5. Archived code runs with the archived data** | Code must be able to run without error using the archived data. With the exception of easy to fix file path errors, all errors should be addressed by the author. |
| **6. Results can be computationally reproduced by running the archived code** | Results reproduced by the data editor with the archived data and code must match those presented in the manuscript. A tolerance threshold can be given when there is not an exact match but the authors must state clearly in the code metadata why this mismatch might occur. If saved model outputs are instead provided, this must also be clearly stated in the metadata. |

### How TADA maps onto the stages {#sortee-tada-map}

Wiki guidance. TADA covers the author-side work for Stages 1 and 3 almost
exactly:

| TADA | SORTEE stages |
|---|---|
| **Transferable** | 1.4 and 3.4 (interoperable formats) and, in practice, 5 (code runs, since local file paths are the most common cause of failure) |
| **Available** | 1.1 and 3.1 (open repository, PID, cited in the manuscript) |
| **Documented** | 1.2, 1.5, 3.2 and 3.5 (licence and metadata) |
| **Annotated** | 3.5 (sectioned code with clear annotation and signposting), and it is what makes Stage 4 assessable at all |
| *(Not TADA: your responsibility as author)* | 1.3 and 3.3 (completeness), 2 (data matches manuscript), 6 (results reproduce) |

### Common failures at each stage {#sortee-common-failures}

Drawn from the guidelines' own account of common problems.

**Stage 5, code runs.** The most frequent causes of failure are:

- a package or module not installed or loaded within the code
- a missing code chunk
- variable names in the code not matching those in the data files
- code referencing data files whose names do not match the archived files
- **local or absolute file paths**, singled out as one of the most common
  reasons that code does not run

::: {.tada-note}
Data editors are told to be pragmatic about paths. An absolute path, or a way of
specifying relative paths they are not familiar with, **should not** be a reason
to return the code, provided they can make it run with minor changes. It is
logged as a **minor error**. Every other error is the author's to correct, and
it is explicitly not the data editor's job to make your code run.
:::

**Stage 6, results reproduce.** In most cases exact reproducibility is expected:
the exact number in the manuscript should come out of the code. State any of the
following legitimate reasons for a mismatch in the metadata:

- **Stochastic methods** such as simulations and MCMC. Set a seed (`set.seed()`
  in R, `random.seed()` in Python) **at the beginning of any code section that
  would be run independently**, including for figure generation with jittering.
  Note that setting a seed does not *always* guarantee reproducibility.
- **Post-processing of figures in other software.** The data in the figure are
  still expected to be the same, but the code may not reproduce the figure
  exactly.
- **Software version differences.** If results are sensitive to the version
  used, flag it clearly and justify the version in the manuscript and metadata.

**Computationally expensive or proprietary analyses.** Where code needs
specialist hardware, takes a very long time, or depends on proprietary software
such as ASReml, full computational reproducibility cannot be assessed. In those
cases:

- Indicate it clearly in the metadata, **alongside a saved output**, for example
  large Bayesian model objects saved as `.rds`
- Ideally provide **example code** demonstrating that the code will run, such as
  an analysis on a subset of the data, or a model run for a reduced duration
- Where only part of the analysis needs proprietary software, say **which**
  parts a data editor can assess
- Consider non-proprietary execution routes, such as GNU Octave for MATLAB code
  or MATLAB Compiler for standalone applications, but test compatibility and
  note any limitations in the metadata
- Build systems such as **`targets`** (R) or **Snakemake** can provide
  reproducibility signatures (hashes) for computationally intensive steps, along
  with intermediate data objects

## Advice for authors {#sharing-authors}

The guidelines' own suggestions, which are the highest-return habits here.

**1. Adhere to the guidelines from the beginning of the study.** Making a
project accessible and reproducible at the *end* is a great deal of work. Create
a clear directory structure and a README at the start, and update the metadata
as new files are added. Annotate code as you produce it. Working with
reproducibility in mind also makes it far more likely that someone else can
reuse the project and successfully run the code, which matters a great deal if
several people will touch the study over its lifetime.

**2. Prepare data and code before submission to any journal.** Having it ready
minimises problems during submission and quality control, and makes transfer to
another journal straightforward if the paper is rejected.

**3. Perform a pre-submission code review.** Send the project to a colleague or
co-author before submitting. They can check that the code runs with the data in
the structure provided, that the metadata is adequate, that data and code match
the manuscript, and that results reproduce. Co-authors are also more likely to
spot mistakes *in* the code, because they know the study and the data, and data
editors do not check code reliability. See [Code review](#code-review).

**4. Consider Markdown or Quarto.** Presenting everything in one self-contained
document is very helpful for data editors and future readers
([Buckley et al. 2025]{.tada-cite key="buckley-2025"}), because it makes
the link between code, data and outputs explicit.

::: {.tada-tip}
**Say what was checked.** If your journal performs quality control, the
guidelines suggest stating this in the data and code availability section, for
example: *"Data and code were checked from Stage 1–4 of the SORTEE guidelines
for Data and Code Quality Control"*. Note explicitly where a check could not be
performed, whether because of proprietary software, sensitive data or
computationally expensive analyses.
:::

## Checklist {#sharing-checklist}

- [ ] Raw data are archived, or a documented reason and route to them is given (option a, b or c)
- [ ] Processed and filtered data are archived, or the code that produces them is
- [ ] All data are in interoperable formats (`.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` or `.parquet` preferred)
- [ ] Any proprietary-format file is accompanied by an interoperable extract and a description of the conversion, including software version
- [ ] Nothing lives only in supplementary material
- [ ] A data licence is chosen and stated
- [ ] A code licence is chosen and stated
- [ ] The README covers manuscript, authors, contact, collection date and location, funders, licence, and derived-data sources
- [ ] Every variable in every data file is described, **with units**
- [ ] Data and code deposits are cited in the text and the reference list
- [ ] All code used to generate results is archived, covering filtering, processing, graphing and analysis
- [ ] Seeds are set before anything stochastic
- [ ] Saved outputs are provided for anything slow or proprietary, and flagged in the metadata
- [ ] LLM use in code generation is disclosed in the README
